cards.front: What is climate change?
back: A long-term change in average climate conditions.

cards.front: Name one source of evidence for past climate.
back: Ice cores.

cards.front: Name the greenhouse gas released in large quantities by burning fossil fuels.
back: Carbon dioxide.

cards.front: What sea temperature is normally needed for a tropical storm to form?
back: About 27°C or above.

cards.front: What is agricultural drought?
back: A shortage of soil moisture for crops and grazing.

cards.front: Name the ocean-atmosphere event linked to Australia's 2002–03 drought.
back: El Niño.

cards.front: Explain how ice cores provide climate evidence.
back: Trapped air bubbles preserve past greenhouse-gas concentrations.
Oxygen isotopes in the ice indicate past temperature.

cards.front: Give two human causes of increased greenhouse-gas emissions.
back: Burning fossil fuels.
Deforestation, farming, landfill or fertiliser use.

cards.front: Explain why tropical storms weaken over land.
back: The storm loses its supply of warm ocean water and moisture.
Friction over land also disrupts its rotating winds.

cards.front: Give two effects of climate change on people.
back: Greater heat-related illness or water shortage.
Damage to homes, food supply or infrastructure from extremes and sea-level rise.

cards.front: Give two effects of Australia's 2002–2009 drought.
back: Farm production and income fell.
Reservoirs and river flows declined, or bushfire risk increased.

cards.front: Give two Australian adaptations to drought.
back: Water restrictions or recycling.
Desalination, efficient irrigation, water trading or changing farm practice.

cards.front: Explain how volcanic eruptions can cause short-term cooling.
back: Large eruptions send ash and sulphur aerosols high into the atmosphere.
These reflect part of the Sun's energy back to space.
Less solar energy reaches the surface, causing temporary cooling.

cards.front: Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect.
back: Earth gives out long-wave heat radiation.
Extra greenhouse gases absorb and re-radiate more of this heat.
Less energy escapes to space, so average temperature rises.

cards.front: Explain why many hot deserts occur around 30° north and south.
back: Air that rose near the Equator moves poleward and cools.
It sinks around 30°, creating high pressure.
Sinking air prevents clouds and rainfall, producing dry conditions.

cards.front: Explain how El Niño can contribute to Australian drought.
back: Warm Pacific water and rising air shift eastwards.
Rainfall is displaced away from the western Pacific.
Eastern and northern Australia therefore face a higher chance of dry winter and spring conditions.

cards.front: Explain one strength and one limitation of tree rings as climate evidence.
back: Strength: annual rings can be accurately dated and their width records favourable or difficult growing seasons.
Limitation: growth is affected by rainfall, disease and local conditions as well as temperature.

cards.front: Explain two conditions needed for a tropical storm to develop.
back: Sea temperature above about 27°C supplies rapid evaporation and latent heat when water condenses.
Low wind shear allows a tall rotating storm structure to build instead of being torn apart.

cards.front: Explain two environmental effects of prolonged drought.
back: Low river flow and shrinking wetlands destroy aquatic habitats and reduce water quality.
Dry vegetation and exposed soil increase wildfire risk and erosion.

cards.front: Explain why Australia's Millennium Drought became severe even though not every year was an El Niño year.
back: Repeated failures of cool-season rainfall produced a cumulative shortage in soil, rivers and reservoirs.
High temperatures and evaporation increased water loss, so occasional rain did not fully restore long-term stores.
